name: Elevated head sleeping / wedge pillow
lead: Sleeping with the head raised, using a wedge pillow, stacked pillows or blocks under the head of the bed, is a way people try to wake up with a less puffy face. Looksmaxxing and skincare communities say that keeping the head above the body overnight limits fluid pooling around the eyes and cheeks, so the face looks more defined in the morning. [3]

Wikipedia's article on periorbital puffiness notes that eye swelling is typically most noticeable right after waking, that lying flat lets fluid shift toward the face, and that elevating the head is a commonly suggested way to limit the pooling. [3] The same article lists other contributors, such as salt-heavy meals, alcohol, allergies, poor sleep and ageing. [3]

Head-of-bed elevation is also an established non-drug measure for gastro-oesophageal reflux, and wedge pillows have been tested in trials for that purpose. [1][2] No published trial has tested a wedge pillow for facial puffiness or appearance. Head-up sleeping has also been studied in obstructive sleep apnea, where a 2025 multicenter observational study measured breathing during sleep at a 30-degree head-of-bed angle.[13]
infobox: Foam wedge pillow, stacked pillows, bed risers, adjustable base

paras: A wedge pillow is a triangular foam cushion that slopes the upper body. Wikipedia lists it among orthopedic pillows and notes that wedge pillows are mainly used to relieve acid reflux and GERD symptoms during sleep, though they are multipurpose. [6] Other ways to achieve the same slope include blocks under the head-end bed legs and adjustable beds. [1]

Wedges are also used for comfort. On T Nation's training forum, members have suggested a wedge to support the head and shoulders for side sleepers with shoulder discomfort, and one reported wedging a pillow behind their back to avoid crushing a lower shoulder. [7][8]

Common forms are a one-piece foam wedge placed under the upper body, a stack of ordinary pillows, risers or blocks under the head-end legs of the bed frame, and adjustable bases that tilt the mattress. Wikipedia's reflux article describes raising the head of the bed on 6-inch blocks as one lifestyle measure, and notes the same advice is given during pregnancy.[12] Wedges that support only the head can bend the neck forward, whereas ones that slope the whole torso keep the spine in one line; this difference is a design point rather than something the studies compare.[1]

While upright, gravity pulls fluid toward the lower body. Lying flat removes that pull, and Wikipedia says this lets fluid move toward the face, which is why puffiness is most obvious on waking. [3] Elevating the head is described there as a way to limit the pooling around the eyes. [3]

Researchers have measured a related effect in the eye. A 2014 prospective, nonrandomised comparison of 30 patients (15 with glaucoma, 15 without) in a sleep laboratory found nocturnal intraocular pressure was on average 1.51 mm Hg lower at a 20-degree head-up position on a wedge pillow than lying flat, an 8 to 9 percent reduction. [4] This shows that the position changes fluid-related pressures in the head, though it measured eye pressure rather than appearance.

Wikipedia's article on sleep positions says raising the head lowers oesophageal acid exposure and acid clearance time, and notes that positional therapy that discourages back sleeping may reduce snoring.[11] The same article reports that positional obstructive sleep apnea, which improves when back sleeping is avoided, accounts for an estimated 56 to 75 percent of obstructive sleep apnea cases.[11]

In looksmaxxing and skincare circles the wedge is paired with other depuffing habits, such as lower evening salt and alcohol intake, cold compresses and facial massage in the morning. Wikipedia lists cold compresses and diet adjustment alongside head elevation as ways to manage puffiness. [3]

A 2021 systematic review of head-of-bed elevation for reflux screened 1,206 records and included five trials with 228 patients (two with bed blocks, one with a wedge pillow, two with both). All five were judged at high risk of performance bias and the trials were too varied for meta-analysis, but the four that reported reflux symptoms found improvement with elevation; a high-quality crossover trial showed a clinically important reduction in symptom scores at 6 weeks. [1]

A 2026 noninferiority randomised trial in 24 patients with persistent nocturnal reflux despite morning PPI compared adding a wedge pillow with adding an evening PPI for 4 weeks. At week 4 symptom questionnaire scores were 30.0 in the wedge group and 36.3 in the twice-daily PPI group. [2] A separate 2025 randomised trial of 256 patients tested an ergonomic wedge pillow during prone ERCP and found less next-day neck pain (19% vs 30%). [9]

A 2025 prospective multicenter study enrolled 30 people with obstructive sleep apnea and 30 healthy controls and recorded polysomnography supine, with the bed head raised 30 degrees and on the side. In the apnea group the apnea-hypopnea index fell from 25.7 supine to 17.8 with head elevation, and to 14.8 on the side; sleep efficiency rose from 73.0 to 79.0 percent with elevation, and half of the apnea patients had at least a 50 percent reduction in the index.[13] Better sleep is itself one of the factors Wikipedia lists among contributors to puffy-looking eyes, which is how some users link sleep-position aids to morning appearance.[3]

Wedge use is generally low-risk. Wikipedia's overview of orthopedic pillows notes that side sleeping puts pressure on shoulders and arms and that back sleeping may favour snoring and back pain, which is why pillow shape and support matter for comfort. [6] Persistent or severe facial swelling can indicate an underlying condition and warrants medical evaluation, according to Wikipedia. [3]

Reflux-related guidance on head elevation distinguishes a sloped torso from simply stacking pillows under the head, and users with neck or shoulder problems describe tailoring the slope to comfort.[1][7] Wikipedia's puffiness article lists allergies as the most common cause of eyelid swelling and several medical conditions among causes, so a sudden or lasting change in swelling is generally evaluated by a clinician.[3]
No studies found for facial puffiness or appearance.
Related trials exist for reflux (five trials in a 2021 review; a 2026 noninferiority trial), for neck pain after ERCP, and for nocturnal intraocular pressure at 20-degree head-up. [1][2][4][9]

timeline.event: The wedge pillow is described in the American Journal of Nursing as a device for maintaining hyperextension of the spine. [10]
Sleep-laboratory study reports lower nocturnal intraocular pressure at 20-degree head-up. [4]
Systematic review of head-of-bed elevation for reflux published. [1]
Multicenter study reports lower apnea-hypopnea index with 30-degree head-of-bed elevation in people with obstructive sleep apnea.[13]
Noninferiority trial compares wedge pillow with evening PPI for nocturnal reflux. [2]

lore.intro: Elevated sleeping is discussed in depuffing and sleep routines, and on T Nation mostly as a comfort aid for lifters. [7][8]

claims.claim: Sleeping with the head raised reduces morning facial puffiness
claims.believers: Proponents say fluid drains away from the face when the head is above the heart overnight, and describe less swelling around the eyes on waking. [3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes head elevation as a way to limit fluid pooling around the eyes; no trial has tested wedge pillows for facial appearance. [3]

claims.claim: A wedge pillow eases reflux and nighttime discomfort
claims.believers: Users report that raising the upper body helps them sleep more comfortably. [7]
claims.experts: A 2021 systematic review of five small trials found symptom improvement with head-of-bed elevation, and a 2026 noninferiority trial tested a wedge against an evening PPI. [1][2]

claims.claim: Raising the head can reduce snoring and sleep-apnea events
claims.believers: Users who sleep propped up describe quieter, more comfortable nights, and sleep-position advice often pairs elevation with side sleeping.[7]
claims.experts: A 2025 observational study of 60 participants found a lower apnea-hypopnea index at 30 degrees of head elevation in people with obstructive sleep apnea; side sleeping showed the lowest value.[13]

claims.claim: A wedge helps side sleepers with shoulder discomfort
claims.believers: T Nation members have suggested a wedge for the head and shoulders, and one lifter reported leaning back against a wedged pillow to stop crushing a lower shoulder.[7][8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's orthopedic-pillow overview notes side sleeping puts pressure on the shoulders and arms and that pillow shape affects comfort; no trial cited tests wedges for shoulder discomfort.[6]

card.summary: Raising the head while asleep to cut morning puffiness; proven for reflux, untested for looks.

quick.overview:
Wedge pillows raise the head during sleep. They are used for reflux.

Some say they reduce morning facial puffiness; no trial tests this.
quick.mechanism: Elevation is thought to limit fluid shifting toward the face while lying flat.
quick.risks: Low risk; one reflux trial and a review exist, none on appearance.

chain: Head and upper body stay raised overnight
Less fluid shifts toward the face and eyes while lying down
Less morning puffiness, so a sharper-looking face on waking
angle.text: People use a wedge pillow or raised bed head to wake up with less swelling around the eyes and cheeks. The mechanism is gravity-assisted fluid drainage, described in reference sources, and it takes effect while sleeping with no products involved.
